stages.a: A colonized block. An X is cut through the bag on its face.
stages.v: Blue oysters are opened with side slits or X cuts.

stages.a: A tight knot of pins pushes out through the cut.
stages.v: Staple species fruit at 13-18 °C. At 13 °C fruit grows slower and denser; at 18 °C, faster.

stages.a: The caps fan out in an overlapping shelf. Their edges still roll under.
stages.v: High CO2 gives long stems and no caps. Watch stem length and cap shape as your airflow gauge.

stages.a: The caps are open wide, the edges still turned down a little.
stages.v: Pick before the caps flatten. A good room gives short stems and flattening caps, not vase shapes.

stages.a: The caps flatten out and their edges lift and wave.
stages.v: Flat caps mean the pick is past: oysters are picked before the caps flatten.

stages.a: The edges turn up and split, and the gills shed spores.
stages.v: Spore load matters for staff health. Choosing strains for it cuts spores, but no oyster is truly spore-less.

labels.a: The cut in the bag. The cluster comes out here.
A tight knot of pins at the cut.
labels.v: Blotch shows first on the centre pin of a budding cluster, and on aborted pins at its base.

labels.a: Short, thick stems, off-centre, joined at the base.
labels.v: Short stems mean good airflow. High CO2 gives long stems with small caps or none.

labels.a: A young cap keeps its edge rolled under.
A shell-shaped cap, streaked out from where it joins the stem.
labels.v: In some strains colour tracks temperature: Steel Blue came out near white when hot and deep blue when cold.

labels.a: Gills run down from the cap onto the stem.
The cap opens flat and its edge lifts.
The edge curls up and splits as the cap ages.
Spores drift down from the gills.
labels.v: Spore load matters for staff health.
